newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Old Mutual seeking further asset swaps.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Old Mutual seeking further asset swaps.

text.p: Old Mutual, South Africa's biggest life assurer, said on Monday it was actively seeking asset swaps to raise the foreign exposure of its flagship Investor's Fund to the 10 percent Reserve Bank limit.
Selwyn Feldman, managing director of Old Mutual Unit Trusts, said there was growing investor interest in funds with significant offshore exposure.
"We have indicated our desire to take the Investor's Fund up to the 10 percent limit as soon as possible and we are actively looking for asset swap opportunities," he told Reuters.
Feldman said the Investor's Fund, which, at 5.6 billion rand, is currently South Africa's largest unit trust fund, would remain premdominantly domestic.
"We are going to drive towards the 10 percent level and in the absence of exchange controls, we would take that up to around 15 percent of total assets invested abroad," he said.

The Investor's Fund currently has about 2.5 percent of assets, equivalent to around 140 million rand, invested abroad, but Old Mutual recently announced agreement with an offshore partner on a 200 million rand asset swap.
The group would have to arrange additional asset swaps worth more than another 200 million to reach the full 560 million exposure mooted by Feldman.
Asset swaps are currently the only mechanism approved by the Reserve Bank for institutional investment abroad.
Feldman said Old Mutual's Global Equity Fund had already reached the threshold imposed by the central Reserve Bank in terms of South Africa's remaining foreign exchange controls.

But he said that with 1.5 million rand a day flowing in from investors positioning themselves for the next step in the phasing out of restrictions on investment abroad by South African residents, the fund's assets were expected to pass 400 million rand soon.
Feldman said he expected the unit trust industry to agree soon on prudential guidelines to be applied after the dismantling of exchange controls.
"We have already done quite a lot of work on the classification of funds - domestic, foreign or specialty.... We're quite far down the road on setting the upper limits that would apply," he said.
He said that while there was unlikely to be any latitude across sectoral boundaries, all sectors would be allowed to invest the same percentage of assets abroad.
"A gold fund would have to stay in gold... but there would be an upper limit for a domestic fund investing abroad. I think we're looking at a figure of around 20 percent to 25 percent," he said.

Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals and Finance Minister Trevor Manuel have both referred recently to a need for prudential regulations to protect South Africa's savings when exchange controls are dismantled.
